section_summary: This section consists chiefly of Federal Communications Commission transcripts of Dōmei press broadcasts intercepted in July 1943, together with two forwarding letters to Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle Jr. The broadcasts combine Japanese war claims from the Solomon Islands and North China with reports promoting the administration and impending independence of Burma and the Philippines, economic mobilization, scientific and agricultural projects, and Subhas Chandra Bose’s Indian independence movement. A recurring propaganda theme is condemnation of the Allied bombing of Rome, while several transmissions repeat naval spokesman Kengo Tominaga’s analysis of American Pacific strategy. Two intercepts preserve the Japanese broadcasts in romanized Japanese rather than translation.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press intercept: Macau, sweet-potato fiber, and Ba Maw’s return from Shōnan
subfiles.from: Dōmei News Agency, via a Japanese radio station
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: A continuing Dōmei broadcast reports on Macau’s economy, a Japanese textile-fiber invention, and Ba Maw’s consultations with Japanese and Indian independence leaders.
subfiles.summary: The Macau dispatch describes the neutral Portuguese territory’s multinational population, dependence on gambling and opium revenue, circulation of numerous currencies, and the decline of the Hong Kong dollar against Japanese military scrip. A Shizuoka item credits Izumi Sasaki with extracting usable fiber from fermented sweet-potato stalks. The longest report quotes Ba Maw on preparations for Burmese independence, cooperation with Hideki Tōjō and Subhas Chandra Bose, and Burma’s military role on the frontier with India.

subfiles.title: FCC letter forwarding additional Dōmei Press intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Sterling forwards additional copies of Dōmei Press broadcasts intercepted from Japanese stations.
subfiles.summary: The confidential letter identifies FCC file 12718 and State Department file 894.76/143. Sterling transmits the attached intercept copies by special messenger in his capacity as chief of the Radio Intelligence Division.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press intercepts: North China campaign and Japanese naval claims
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: French- and English-language Dōmei broadcasts cover Asian students at Karuizawa, Japanese operations in North China, a new naval spokesman, and air fighting in the Solomon Islands.
subfiles.summary: The first transmission describes Southeast Asian students at Karuizawa and gives expansive Japanese claims for casualties, prisoners, captured weapons, and Chinese commanders joining the Nanjing government in North China. A later item introduces Captain Etsuzō Kurihara as successor to Captain Hideo Hiraide in the Imperial Headquarters Navy Press Section. Further reports claim heavy Allied aircraft losses and damage at Roviana, Guadalcanal, Tulagi, Vanikoro, Buin, and Bougainville while minimizing Japanese losses.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press broadcast of July 19: military, economic, and occupied-Asia reports
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: A multi-item broadcast reports Japanese military communiqués and speeches alongside economic, scientific, and independence-related stories from Japan and occupied Asia.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast repeats Japanese casualty and matériel claims from North China and the Solomon Islands, including operations at Roviana, Buin, New Georgia, the Ai River, and Munda. Tōjō addresses a gubernatorial conference on total mobilization, food self-sufficiency, and preparation for a decisive offensive. Other dispatches concern rice prospects, reclamation of the Yangtze delta, the Makassar research institute, an Indian boy’s donation to Subhas Chandra Bose’s movement, a Malayan delegation to Japan, and a Manila editorial attacking Wendell Willkie’s One World.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press intercept: New Georgia fighting, enemy patents, and the bombing of Rome
subfiles.from: Dōmei News Agency, Japanese radio transmission
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The transmission combines reports from Shōnan and Manila with detailed Japanese claims about New Georgia, disposal of Allied patents, and reactions to the bombing of Rome.
subfiles.summary: Early items describe a Malayan inspection party, graduates of the Kalibapi Labor Training Institute, Captain Kurihara’s debut, and Japanese accounts of fighting around the Ai River and Munda. Another report announces the disposal of patents and trademarks owned by nationals of enemy countries. The final pages condemn the first Allied bombing of Rome and begin a badly faded item on awards for Japanese seamen.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press intercepts: Catholic reactions, Burma appointment, Tonkin raids, and Shōnan health
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: A group of July 20 broadcasts reports anti-Allied Catholic reactions to the bombing of Rome and administrative developments across Burma, China, Indochina, and Shōnan.
subfiles.summary: Manila clergy William Piani and César María Guerrero denounce the bombing of Rome and the Basilica of San Lorenzo, while a Legazpi report depicts it as an attack on Catholicism. Renzo Sawada discusses his appointment to assist preparations for Burmese independence, and another item names a new army air-force commander. Additional dispatches cover American bombing of Haiphong and Tonkin, transfer of former British and American property at Hankou, and Japanese claims to have eliminated epidemic diseases in Shōnan.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press intercepts: Tominaga’s Pacific analysis and French-language occupied-Asia reports
subfiles.from: Dōmei News Agency, stations JAP/JUP and JUO/JAU2
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The packet centers on Kengo Tominaga’s analysis of American Pacific strategy and includes French-language reports on Japanese programs in Southeast Asia and China.
subfiles.summary: Tominaga argues that the United States has always followed a “Pacific first” policy but that Japan retains strategic superiority; he describes Australia, Hawaii, Canton, Samoa, Guadalcanal, and New Guinea as components of an American supply and defense system. French-language items discuss Indonesian naval trainees at Makassar, Shōnan disease control, the Hankou property transfer, Catholic criticism of the Rome raid, and American bombing in Tonkin. The final page begins a repeat of the Tominaga commentary.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press compilation: Vatican protest, Asian independence, appointments, and social conditions
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: English- and French-language broadcasts report diplomatic protests, educational and scientific developments, and Japanese-sponsored independence programs in Burma and the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: The compilation opens with Monsignor Montini’s reported protest to American chargé Harold Tittmann over the bombing of Rome, followed by Philippine university enrollment figures and an editorial supporting Subhas Chandra Bose. It also reports American military psychiatric hospitalization statistics and the research agenda of Ichiro Sonobe’s Makassar institute. Later French and English items cover Jorge Vargas, Prince Yi Geon, Prachon Patchanuk, Renzo Sawada’s career and Burma mission, the Malayan-Sumatran inspection party, Tasuku Ito’s appointment at Shōnan, and propaganda contrasting Japanese and American preparations for Philippine independence.

subfiles.title: FCC letter forwarding additional Dōmei Press intercepts
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Sterling forwards another group of intercepted Dōmei Press broadcasts to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: The confidential special-messenger letter cites FCC file 12718 and State Department file 894.76/144. It repeats the standard notice that additional copies of Dōmei Press intercepted from Japanese stations are attached.

subfiles.title: Romanized Japanese Dōmei intercept: North China food controls and Burmese independence
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: A romanized Japanese broadcast discusses food pricing and anti-hoarding controls in North China and introduces a feature on Burma’s approaching independence.
subfiles.summary: The first two items describe official purchase and sale prices for staple grains in Beijing and Tianjin and threaten severe punishment for merchants concealing food stocks. A third feature presents Burmese independence as the culmination of a century of resistance to British oppression. The transcript remains in romanized Japanese without an English translation.

subfiles.title: Romanized Japanese Dōmei intercept: North China campaign and European food supply
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: A romanized Japanese broadcast presents Japanese military statistics for North China and an Axis-oriented assessment of Europe’s food situation.
subfiles.summary: The first item claims Japanese victories in North China during the first half of 1943, listing engagements, enemy casualties, prisoners, destroyed facilities, and captured weapons. The second argues that Britain’s blockade of Axis-dominated Europe has failed and attributes earlier shortages chiefly to bad weather. It predicts generally normal or improved harvests in Germany and occupied European countries while disputing American claims of acute scarcity.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press intercepts: Pacific operations, Rome bombing, Indian forces, and José Laurel
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The broadcasts report Japanese military claims in the Pacific, propaganda concerning the Rome bombing, the Indian National Army, and Philippine independence leader José P. Laurel.
subfiles.summary: Japanese accounts claim aircraft victories near Buin, the salvage of the King George V floating dock at Seletar, and raids on Canton Island and Vanikoro. Tomokazu Hori and Manila commentators condemn the Allied bombing of Rome, while another item covers the first graduation from an Indian National Army officers’ school attended by Subhas Chandra Bose. The closing report describes José P. Laurel leaving the Philippine General Hospital and returning to work on the proposed Philippine constitution with Ramon Avanceña and other commission members.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press broadcast: Tominaga’s Pacific strategy commentary and domestic mobilization
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: This broadcast repeats Kengo Tominaga’s strategic analysis and adds reports on Japanese regional administration, American labor policy, and Renzo Sawada’s Burma appointment.
subfiles.summary: Tominaga portrays American operations from Hawaii and Australia through the Solomon Islands as a systematic counteroffensive intended to sever Japan’s strategic line, while claiming a continuing four-to-one Japanese aerial advantage. A Tokyo item describes decisions by regional administrative liaison councils on production, food, transport, and delegated authority. The broadcast also reports Paul V. McNutt’s readiness to propose compulsory labor in the United States and repeats Mainichi’s praise of Renzo Sawada as ambassador to Burma.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Press intercept fragment: Bena Bena raid and Laurel’s hospital departure
subfiles.from: Dōmei News Agency, Japanese radio station
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: A fragmentary transmission reports a Japanese raid on Bena Bena and resumes the story of José P. Laurel leaving the Philippine General Hospital.
subfiles.summary: A Lisbon-datelined item claims Japanese bombers attacked the Allied base at Bena Bena in New Guinea. The following Manila dispatch repeats details of Laurel’s recovery, his gift kimono from Eiji Amau, and his exchange with Police Chief Torres while leaving the hospital. The document continues beyond the supplied section.
